title: Distribution of light-matter quantum correlations with a temporally multiplexed solid-state quantum memory array
authors: Aya Mneimneh, Susana Plascencia, Manuel Gundin, Jonathan Hänni, Samuele Grandi, Markus Teller, Hugues de Riedmatten
abstract: Multiplexed quantum memories increase the entanglement distribution rate in long-distance quantum repeater architectures by harnessing storage in several degrees of freedom. Here, we report on the distribution of light-matter quantum correlations using an array of time-multiplexed solid-state quantum memories. We store telecom-heralded single photons sequentially in up to ten memory cells using the full atomic frequency comb protocol with on-demand read-out in a Pr$^{3+}$:Y$_2$SiO$_5$ crystal. Leveraging both spatial and temporal multiplexing, we demonstrate quantum correlations between the telecom photon and up to 60 spatio-temporal modes of the quantum memory array. We then transmit the heralding telecom photon over 39.1 km of deployed optical fiber in the Metropolitan Area of Barcelona. In a realistic scenario where the generation rate is limited by the two-way communication time, we show that up to 15 % of the $393 μs$ round-trip communication time is filled with communication trials, leading to a 60-fold enhancement in the rate of detected telecom photons correlated with the quantum memory array, compared to a single-mode memory. With increased storage times and efficiencies, our multiplexed quantum memory array will constitute the backbone of a long-distance quantum network, establishing remote entanglement at high rates.
summary: This paper reports on distributing light-matter quantum correlations using a highly multiplexed solid-state quantum memory array. By leveraging both spatial and temporal multiplexing, the authors achieved quantum correlations in up to 60 modes and demonstrated a significant rate enhancement for quantum communication over a metropolitan fiber link. This work advances the feasibility of long-distance quantum networks.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is overcoming the fundamental rate limitation in long-distance quantum repeater architectures imposed by classical signaling time.
main_result: The authors demonstrated light-matter quantum correlations in 60 spatio-temporal modes and achieved a 60-fold enhancement in the correlated telecom photon detection rate by utilizing multiplexing over a metropolitan fiber link.
method: Quantum correlations were distributed and measured using a time-multiplexed solid-state quantum memory array (QMA) coupled with a cSPDC source, and the resulting idler photons were sent over a 39.1 km fiber link.
model_or_system: The system uses a quantum memory array based on a Pr3+:Y2SiO5 crystal, employing both spatial (10 cells) and temporal (up to 6 modes/cell) multiplexing via the full atomic frequency comb protocol.
key_observables: Cross-correlations ($g^{(2)}_{s,i}$), coincidence rates ($R_C$), and the rate enhancement factor.
important_parameters: 39.1 km fiber link length, 60 spatio-temporal modes, $393 \mu	ext{s}$ round-trip communication time.
main_assumptions: The experiment operates in a realistic scenario where the generation rate is limited by the round-trip communication time.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup, the temporal sequence of photon storage across multiple memory cells, and plots showing cross-correlations and the rate enhancement vs. the number of modes.
paper_structure: The paper details the experimental setup, the protocol for storing and retrieving photons in the multiplexed QMA, the measurement of quantum correlations both locally and over a long-distance fiber link, and the quantitative analysis of rate enhancement.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the physical implementation challenges of quantum networking by demonstrating high-rate entanglement distribution using solid-state memories, which is crucial for scaling quantum communication infrastructure.

Fig. 2 Experimental sequence. The cSPDC source emits pairs of signal and idler photons within an acceptance window (AW) of 6 µs corresponding to Nt temporal modes. While the idler photon travels to the detector, the first cell Ns = 1 of the QMA absorbs the signal photon. Subsequently, a CP is applied, and the cSPDC pump is switched off. After a storage time Ts = 8 µs, a second CP is applied and leads to re-emission of the signal photon after Ts + τ = 18 µs. The cSPDC is switched on again, and quantum storage continues with the next memory cell. These steps are repeated until storage has been attempted with all memory cells.
